questions.stem: Which term names one species living in one place at one time?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
A community bundles every population, not one species.
A habitat is the place itself, not the group.
An ecosystem adds abiotic factors to the living mix.

questions.stem: Badgers, deer, oak trees and ants share a woodland. What does the woodland represent to them?

options.explanation: Genotype is a genetic term, not a place.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Four species together cannot form one population.
Community names the group of populations, not the place.

questions.stem: What must an ecosystem include that a community does not?

options.explanation: Biotic factors alone are the community part.
Ecosystems can be tiny; scale is not the criterion.

options.text: The abiotic factors, such as light intensity, mineral ions and water availability
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: More species than the community holds
options.explanation: The species set is identical; the factors differ.

questions.stem: What happens to a community if one species is removed?

options.explanation: Interdependence means effects spread.

options.text: Only the removed species is lost
options.explanation: Its partners feel the knock-on effects.
Removal shrinks, not doubles, the community.

options.text: The whole community can be affected, since species depend on each other
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A garden pond and the whole of Antarctica are both examples of what?

options.text: Ecosystems, showing ecosystems vary greatly in size and scale
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Habitats only, since both are places
options.explanation: Both terms apply, but the contrast demonstrates ecosystem scale.
The abiotic factors make them ecosystems.
Each holds many species.

questions.stem: State the definition of a population.
questions.modelAnswer: A population is a group of organisms of one species that live together in one place at one time.

questions.stem: State the definition of an ecosystem.
questions.modelAnswer: An ecosystem is all the biotic factors and abiotic factors interacting within an area at one time.

questions.stem: Explain why a community is more than a population.
questions.modelAnswer: A community is more than a population because it gathers all the populations of every species sharing the area, not just one species at a time.

questions.stem: A student studies all the fish, plants and snails in a pond plus the water and light. Name the terms.
questions.modelAnswer: Each species group is a population, all groups together form the community, the pond is their habitat, and the pond plus its non-living conditions is the ecosystem.
